Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Will you pay for courses that promise your salary will improve by 50% in 3 years (the valuation of her company is hundreds of million dollars and you are promised with a full refund if your salary improves under 50%)?
Answer: No. Thats an impossible claim. The school doesn’t know what I make now, doesn’t control what a future company will pay me, and certainly isn’t in control of my work ethic. It can’t possibly be true for a lot people even if it is true for some students. That screams scam. Marketing should deliver a compelling, believable story and any great storyteller knows to show, not tell. Show me what kind of jobs people who graduate from the courses end up working in, show me the average salaries for those jobs, and show me why companies will make hiring decisions based on the completion of the coursework. I can connect the dots myself. Coursework worth its salt takes time and lots of effort usually in excess of its monetary cost. Even if I believe your garuntee, I still come out a loser if the future employment fails to live up to expectations. Well respected educational institutions are backed by accreditations and a long history of training successful students who go on to do great things. Leave the money back guarantees to electronic devices and focus on teaching the skills that will create tomorrows leaders.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I have been a web application developer for 15 plus years and I want to transition into management. My resume seldom gets picked up for manager positions. What can I do to get a job as a manager?
Answer: Start managing. A title follows the work, it doesn’t precede it. As a developer you should have lots of opportunities to perform administrative tasks no one wants to do and a range of tasks that your manager doesn’t want to do. Do those and do those well and you will be trusted with more. Start with things just outside your role and keep expanding them until there is nothing left or things so large you can’t do them on the side while getting your work done. At that point go to your manager with ideas of how things could be done better and a plan that you will execute that will make things better. Don’t go to them asking for work you have never tried to do. Bring them a complete package and make it hard for them to say no. Explain the expected costs and how to deal with any downsides. Then rinse and repeat until you become a defacto manager. Finally, resumes in general don’t get picked up. If you have 15 years of experience and are handing out resumes to random companies, you have already failed. Use your network. You should have a ton of ex co workers who are familiar with your work and your management abilities who can get your foot in the door. Cold calling with a resume is necessary for individuals straight out of college or when looking to transition to a specific company you would love to work, it’s hard though. Build a reputation for going above and beyond your current role and the opportunities for doing those things will find you.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What happens if a founder, holding minority share, is fired in the first year of a 3-year vesting and 1 year cliff with a double trigger acceleration?
Answer: The founder should consider himself lucky to get out of an obviously abrasive relationship after wasting so little time at the company. As to the double trigger clause those are generally messy. It's not a formal legal term, just one that's spelled out specifically in your employment contract and can really have any terms. It might not be applicable if you were fired preacquisition or have a small timeline in which it applies, like 3 months prior to the acquisition. It may or may not have special terms prior to the cliff. You would have to consult your employment contract knowing specifically what happened to know your rights for sure. In any case, they are meant to be mutually beneficial. The new company knows a specific amount it will take to keep the old employees and the employees have a large payout to keep them at a company they never directly agreed to work for. They work when all parties want to move forward and both make it clear of the cost of the acquisition and to protect you if things go south after it. That being said, prior to the acquisition, if the acquiring company doesn’t actually want the employees or they only care about a scant few of the remaining founders who hold all the voting power, there are seven ways from sunday to get around it. They can simply dissolve all common stock and make an all cash offer for the company or simply devalue the common stock. If there is no stock left, there’s nothing to vest… Basically if the new company has a lawyer on retainer and both the other founders and the new company are intent on not paying you, a double trigger clause, probably isn’t going to save you.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How many lines of code do professional programmers write per hour?
Answer: For the application I wrote for a startup I founded I wrote about a million lines of code over 4 or so years. Or around 100 lines an hour. When I worked for a government contractor on an application where safety was the top priority and people would die if there was a serious bug in production, the government target was 7 lines of code a day and quite frankly it was difficult to average much higher then that. Of course I would usually be quite prolific on some days then do almost nothing for several more as things were designed, reviewed and reviewed again. So to answer your question, I would say it’s perfectly acceptable to write anywhere between 1 and 100 lines of code an hour. Context matters, but even then, at the end of the day, it’s not a metric that matters much. On some refactoring projects, I can often delete more code then I add while optimizing the things I actually care about. What you should care about is how well the end product works, how long it took to get there, and how well it scales over time. The best practical metrics I would say make you a good professional programmer would be do you consistently hit the release dates you set for yourself and does it get easier to do more challenging things over time. If both those things are true, don’t overanalyze it, just keep doing what you are doing no matter how many lines it takes!
